items.description: Una pluma de ganso puso fin a la muerte que había puesto fin a las conversaciones Seguir leyendo

items.title: Estudiantes reclutados por Telegram, saboteadores amateur y sicarios: así externaliza Rusia sus operaciones en Europa
items.description: La noche del 20 de marzo de 2024, especialmente húmeda y templada en Londres, tres veinteañeros se plantaron en un polígono industrial del este de la ciudad a bordo de un Kia Picanto rojo cereza. Entraron, prendieron fuego a un almacén y grabaron el incendio con un teléfono móvil. El vídeo de las llamas devorando el local acabó en manos de otro joven de 20 años, Dylan Earl, captado a través de la aplicación de mensajería Telegram por la organización paramilitar rusa Wagner, de la órbita del Kremlin, y que a su vez había reclutado a otros para hacer el trabajo sucio. Una de las naves incendiadas contenía ayuda humanitaria y equipos de satélite Starlink destinados a Ucrania. Según la investigación británica, los tres jóvenes que prendieron la mecha no sabían que trabajaban en realidad para Rusia. Seguir leyendo

items.title: El asalto de Trump al Supremo de Estados Unidos entra en un año decisivo
items.description: La tradición dicta que el primer lunes de octubre marca el inicio de los nueve meses del curso judicial del Tribunal Supremo de Estados Unidos. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Luis Har, exrehén israelí: “Si hubiese sido solo por nuestro Gobierno, aún habría secuestrados en Gaza”
items.description: Luis Har (Buenos Aires, 73 años) hace un hueco en medio de sus vacaciones en un hotel en Eilat, la turística ciudad a orillas del mar Rojo, en la punta más meridional de Israel. Es la mejor prueba del vuelco —de ciudadano anónimo a personaje público que encadena viajes — que ha dado su vida desde el 7 de octubre de 2023, cuando Hamás lo tomó rehén en su masivo ataque sorpresa, junto con su pareja, Clara Marman, y tres familiares de ella, en un kibutz cercano a Gaza, Nir Itsjak. Los cinco, con doble nacionalidad argentina e israelí. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Vidas de adulto, sueños de niño: el limbo de los adolescentes que cruzaron a Ceuta
items.description: No tienen cama, pero sueñan. Cada noche, Ayman y Zarkariya, de 16 años, buscan un escondrijo en el barrio ceutí de El Príncipe donde no haya militares, ni portales de viviendas, ni demasiada luz. Se enroscan en sus sábanas gemelas e intentan dormir. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Fondos buitre, turistas y alquileres imposibles: ¿qué tipo de ciudad queremos?
items.description: “Madrid / nos pertenece / a ti y a mí”. Aplíquese a Madrid, o a cualquier otra ciudad. Es un verso de Biznaga, la célebre banda de punk rock, conocida por sus letras críticas, siempre atentas a los trances sociopolíticos. El pasado domingo 27 de septiembre, en la acampada por la vivienda en la madrileña Puerta del Sol, se comprobó que es uno de los estribillos que, con los brazos en alto, el público más corea. Hay algo ahí que importa. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Ascensión, la isla desértica que se hizo selva
items.description: Casi en el punto exacto en mitad del Atlántico entre África y América del Sur, si trazáramos una línea por debajo del ecuador, existe una isla que hace 200 años estaba deshabitada y era, según un escritor de la época, “la abominación de la desolación”. “Ascensión solo produce tortugas, ratas e insomnio”, dijo otro. “La tierra más desolada y yerma (como una tierra maldita por Dios) que jamás vieron mis ojos… Creo que el mundo entero no ofrece otro pedazo de suelo semejante”, añadió otro más. Ascensión está tan lejos (1.100 kilómetros del lugar más cercano, la isla de Santa Elena; 1.600 del punto más cercano en África, y 2.300 de Brasil) que no llegó ni una sola semilla de ninguna planta hasta que los humanos, británicos en concreto, se asentaron en ella. “No hay tierra, no hay sombras, no hay plantas, no hay agua”, escribió uno de sus primeros habitantes. Y, sin embargo, Ascensión tiene una enorme importancia geoestratégica desde que fue descubierta y, a pesar de esa desolación, o precisamente por ella, ahora tiene un gigantesco valor medioambiental. También pasó por allí otro famosísimo escritor, científico y revolucionario de la biología, Charles Darwin. Gracias a él y a una historia de coraje, cabezonería, biología e ingeniería, esta isla improbable podría contener el secreto de la lucha contra la desertificación en el mundo, y un joven científico español está trabajando para probarlo. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Y de repente el país se reseteó: cuando vivir cuesta más que los salarios
items.description: Se los ve a los dos cómodos, caminando solos por Central Park. Quizá son los dos líderes más importantes que le quedan a la socialdemocracia en el mundo. Ambos llevan traje azul y sin corbata, y están en Nueva York para intervenir en la asamblea general de las Naciones Unidas del pasado septiembre. Son Andy Burnham, primer ministro de Gran Bretaña y líder laborista, y Pedro Sánchez, presidente del Gobierno español y secretario general del PSOE. Este último todavía no sabe la que le va a caer con el desahucio de su vivienda de una ciudadana octogenaria. Burnham está preparando su intervención —bastante rupturista—, en el congreso anual del Partido Laborista en Liverpool, unos días más tarde. En él declarará : “Esta va a ser nuestra primera ruptura con el pensamiento erróneo de los últimos 40 años. Ya no vamos a contemplar el mercado de la vivienda como un juego de ganadores y perdedores, sino como el bien esencial que todo el mundo necesita para tener una buena vida [lo de “la buena vida, ¿les suena a Keynes?] (…) Con una buena casa todo es posible. Sin una, nada lo parece”. Seguir leyendo

items.title: El apocalipsis laboral de la IA se pospone (por ahora)
items.description: Hay tres versiones del Apocalipsis de San Juan, un texto que nunca pierde vigencia, anticipando los impactos de la inteligencia artificial (IA). Una: la reciente y aterradora perspectiva de la muerte descendiendo de enjambres de máquinas autónomas asesinas impulsadas por la IA , en un trasunto del 2001 de Stanley Kubrik. Dos: un sector cuyas expectativas imposibles está hinchando la madre de todas las burbujas financieras hasta niveles que ríete tú de la Gran Recesión y sus uvas de la ira. Y tres: el fin del trabajo, la reconversión brutal y, a lo peor, la desaparición de millones de empleos , empezando por primera vez en la historia por los de la gente más formada, que puede llevar a la economía global camino de una depresión, a niveles de desigualdad imposibles y a una mezcla de tecnofatalismo, resentimiento y rabia (algo que ya sucede, dicho así entre paréntesis, pero elevado a la enésima potencia). Las utopías y las distopías son máquinas de novelar. Escupen titulares con pegada, latigazos líricos plagados de esdrújulas finiseculares y de sílabas hinchadas como nubes de tormenta. Pero a menudo impiden ver lo que de veras está pasando: que esas visiones hiperbólicas son interesadas. La mayor parte de esos miedos los están inoculando las propias empresas o los gobernantes que las protegen, pensando en su poder y en su cuenta de resultados. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Brasil decide su futuro entre Lula y Bolsonaro, un estadista desgastado y el hijo de un ultra
items.description: Brasil celebra este domingo unas elecciones presidenciales y legislativas que son el tercer duelo electoral consecutivo entre la izquierda democrática que representa Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva y la extrema derecha de los Bolsonaro. Cambian los protagonistas pero no la sustancia. Lula, de 80 años, proclama que el pueblo está llamado “a elegir entre democracia y barbarie”; el senador Flávio Bolsonaro , de 45, eleva la batalla a confrontación “entre el Bien contra el Mal”. Los comicios son un mano a mano entre un estadista desgastado que busca un cuarto mandato, y el heredero político, investigado por corrupción, de un movimiento político ultra. Un aspirante al que se adhieren conservadores y todo el que odia a Lula . El ambiente es de apatía aunque los favoritos llevan meses empatados en las encuestas, proponen modelos antagónicos de país y, literalmente, no quedan casi indecisos. Es muy improbable, pero no imposible, que la elección presidencial quede decidida esta noche. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Viaje a Ningde, la ciudad china convertida en capital mundial de las baterías para coches eléctricos
items.description: Zhong Zihao, de 20 años, ha escuchado que los alrededores del lago Chijian (sureste de China) fueron tierras de cultivo antes de que los arrozales cedieran terreno a las fábricas. Cuesta imaginar aquel paisaje entre las naves industriales, los puentes, las carreteras y los edificios que ahora se levantan a orillas del embalse. Zhong sabe que su ciudad natal era uno de los rincones más pobres y menos industrializados de la provincia de Fujian, pero ahora, comenta con orgullo, “cuando me presento, solo tengo que decir que vengo de Ningde , la de CATL ”. “Que una urbe sea recordada gracias a una empresa es, para una localidad pequeña, una enorme fuente de confianza”, destaca. Seguir leyendo

items.title: De simpáticos juguetes a inquietantes criaturas en una pasarela: ¿cuándo empezaron a asustarnos los robots?
items.description: Yumi Nu es una de las modelos más cotizadas del planeta. La estadounidense de origen neerlandés y japonés, sobrina de Steve Aoki , ha sido portada de Sports Illustrated y desfilado para L’Oréal o Victoria’s Secret. El pasado 22 de septiembre, en el Vogue World de Milán , Nu compartió pasarela con un grupo de intrusos sin experiencia previa: cuatro robots humanoides fabricados por la compañía china Unitree Robotics . Seguir leyendo

items.title: State Police Bill hits roadblock in states
items.description: · Edo, Osun, Oyo, Rivers approve, others drag feet · By Clifford Ndujihe, Politics Editor Prologue Unless something decisive happens in the next 12 days, the push for state police, widely canvassed as a response to Nigeria’s worsening security challenges, is facing a fresh hurdle at the state Houses of Assembly, with only four states -Edo, Osun, Oyo and Rivers having so far approved the proposed constitutional amendment . A panoramic view of the entire country and Sunday Vanguard’s checks show that several other state legislatures are yet to commence consideration of the bill, while some have said they are still awaiting its transmission from the National Assembly. The development is raising concerns over the pace of the constitutional amendment process, coming after the National Assembly transmitted the 1999 Constitution (Sixth Alteration) Bill, 2026, to the 36 state Houses of Assembly on September 16, seeking their concurrence. The National Assembly had asked the state legislatures to communicate their resolutions within 30 days. However, the period is an administrative target and not a constitutional deadline. Under Section 9 of the 1999 Constitution, alteration of the Constitution requires approval by at least two-thirds of the 36 state Houses of Assembly, 24 legislatures, before the amendment can proceed to the next stage. With only four states having approved the proposal so far, the measure still requires the support of 20 more Houses of Assembly to meet the constitutional threshold. But the slow pace of consideration, coupled with claims by some assemblies that they have not received the bill, has thrown up questions over the readiness of the state legislatures to meet the National Assembly’s administrative timeline. While some assemblies have commenced legislative processes on the proposal, others appear to be taking their time, potentially prolonging the journey of a reform that has remained a major component of Nigeria’s security debate. South-West: Osun, Oyo approve bill, Ondo, Ekiti, Ogun study draft By Dayo Johnson, Olasunkanmi Akoni, Rotimi Ojomoyela, Shina Abubakar, James Ogunnaike & Adeola Badru State Houses of Assembly in the South-West are at different stages of considering the proposed constitutional amendment to establish state police, with Osun and Oyo approving the bill, while Ondo, Ekiti and Ogun are still examining the draft. Lagos has endorsed the reform in principle and called for its accelerated passage, but its formal approval of the constitutional amendment transmitted by the National Assembly remains unclear. In Ondo State, the House of Assembly has confirmed receipt of the draft amendment from the National Assembly, which has been distributed to the 26 lawmakers for study. The Assembly’s spokesperson and Chairman, House Committee on Information, Olatunji Oshati, said the draft had been read during plenary before being circulated to members for their inputs. Oshati said the lawmakers would deliberate on the document and forward their observations to the National Assembly within a short period. We have received the draft from the National Assembly. We have read it on the floor of the House and subsequently distributed it to the 26 members of the Assembly to study,” he said. He added that the House would consider the amendment under matters of urgent public importance before transmitting its position to the National Assembly. In Ekiti State, the Assembly has also received the draft bill but is yet to begin deliberations. Jide Agbeyo, Special Assistant on Media to the Speaker, Rt. Hon. Adeoye Aribasoye, confirmed receipt of the bill in a letter dated September 16, 2026, saying the House was prepared to commence the necessary legislative processes. According to him, the bill must first undergo administrative procedures before being listed by the House Rules and Business Committee for formal consideration. He assured that the Assembly would give the proposed legislation the necessary attention once the preliminary processes were completed. However, Osun State has approved the bill, with the House of Assembly passing it clause by clause at plenary on September 22, 2026, without altering any of its provisions. The Speaker’s spokesperson, Tiamiyu Olamide, said the resolution had been compiled by the Clerk and signed by the Speaker, Rt. Hon. Adewale Egbedun, for onward transmission to the National Assembly. He said the House was expected to return its resolution within the stipulated 30-day period, adding that arrangements were underway to transmit the document. In Oyo State, the House of Assembly has passed the constitutional amendment bill seeking to establish state police and is preparing to transmit its resolution to the National Assembly. The bill scaled its third reading at plenary on Tuesday after lawmakers constituted themselves into a Committee of the Whole and considered its provisions clause by clause. The sitting was presided over by the Speaker, Adebo Ogundoyin. The lawmakers approved the draft without amendments. In Ogun State, the Assembly has constituted a committee to examine the proposed state police bill ahead of its consideration by the full House. A source in the Assembly, who spoke to Vanguard on condition of anonymity, said no substantive action had been taken on the bill by the chamber. The committee, comprising former Speaker, Olakunle Oluomo, Deputy Speaker, Bolanle Ajayi, and Majority Leader, Yusuf Sherif Abiodun, among others, is expected to scrutinise the draft and submit a report to guide deliberations. The committee is working within a framework established by the House, with its report expected to pave the way for formal consideration of the bill at plenary. In Lagos State, the House of Assembly has publicly endorsed the establishment of state police, describing it as a major step towards addressing the country’s security challenges. At plenary on July 8 and 9, 2026, the Assembly, presided over by Speaker Mudashiru Obasa, unanimously backed the proposed decentralisation of policing and urged the 36 state legislatures to expedite consideration of the constitutional amendment. The resolution followed a motion titled “Support for the Establishment of State Police in Nigeria”, moved by Majority Leader, Noheem Adams, and Stephen Ogundipe, representing Oshodi-Isolo Constituency I. Despite the Assembly’s endorsement, however, the status of the formal legislative approval of the full constitutional amendment package transmitted by the National Assembly remains uncertain. Checks by Sunday Vanguard indicated that the Lagos Assembly was still studying the draft bills, with no publicly confirmed record of a clause-by-clause vote on the entire package or the formal transmission of its resolution to the National Assembly. The Chairman of the House Committee on Information, Stephen Ogundipe, was unavailable for confirmation on the status of the process, while sources in the Assembly said members were still examining the documents ahead of a formal vote. S-South states Rivers, Edo back bill; Delta consults, C/River begins debate, Bayelsa yet to act By Egufe Yafugborhi, Daniel Abia, Ike Uchechukwu, Emem Idio, Ochuko Akuopha & Ozioruva Aliu In the South-South, the Rivers and Edo State Houses of Assembly have endorsed the proposed constitutional amendment for the establishment of state police, while Cross River has commenced consideration of the bill. However, the proposal is yet to receive a formal response from the Bayelsa and Delta State Houses of Assembly, with the latter consulting stakeholders before taking a position. In Rivers, the House, at plenary presided over by Speaker Martin Amaewhule, unanimously endorsed the constitutional amendment transmitted by the National Assembly. Amaewhule, after reading the letter from the Clerk of the National Assembly and presenting the proposed alterations, put the bill to a vote, which lawmakers unanimously supported. He said the decision was informed by the need to strengthen Nigeria’s security architecture and support ongoing security reforms. The Speaker said the bill contains 26 clauses, including 25 alterations involving substitutions to provisions of the principal Act. He said the proposed amendment would provide a constitutional framework for establishing state police services while strengthening the National Assembly’s role in prescribing national minimum policing standards. The House is expected to formally communicate its resolution to the National Assembly. In Edo, the House also granted concurrence to the constitutional amendment. Leading the debate, Majority Leader, Osezua Ojiezele, urged lawmakers to support the proposal. Donald Okogbe said the establishment of state police would create employment opportunities, while Charity Aiguobarueghian said it would strengthen security at the community level. Edosa Richard advocated the creation of an Edo State Police Commission, while Kingsley Ugabi and Maria Edeko said the proposal would help restore peace in communities. The motion for concurrence, moved by Ojiezele and seconded by Minority Leader, Natasha Osawaru, was overwhelmingly carried. Speaker Idaiye Yekini directed the Clerk to forward clean copies of the resolution to the National Assembly. In Cross River, the House has begun consideration of the bill after taking its First Reading. The proposal, titled A Bill for an Act to Amend the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, 1999, to Provide for the Establishment of State Police Services and for Related Matters, seeks to establish state police while retaining the Nigeria Police Force as the Federal Police Service. Speaker Elvert Ayambem said the bill would undergo the normal legislative process of consideration and debate before the House takes a position. In Delta, the Assembly confirmed receipt of the bill but has not disclosed its position. The Speaker’s Chief Press Secretary, Nkem Nwaeke, said the House was consulting critical stakeholders before taking a position. In Bayelsa, the House was yet to debate or vote on the proposed amendment as of September 25. Sources said the bill had been received but lawmakers had not formally considered it. One source attributed the delay to the Assembly’s prolonged absence from plenary, while another said lawmakers were awaiting the governor’s position. The Assembly last sat on August 18. Bill drags in Northern Assemblies •Kano, Kwara, Taraba, Kebbi others yet to receive bill •Yobe, Borno, Nasarawa, Zamfara, Sokoto receive, yet to debate •Plateau begins consideration, Bauchi sets up committee By Soni Daniel, Northern Region Editor, Demola Akinyemi, Ndahi Marama, Peter Duru, Femi Bolaji, Golok Nanmwa, Maryam Abdulaziz Usman, Christopher Ameh, Fauziyya Lawal, Idris Salisu, Edwin Phillip, Hadiza Yusuf, Usman Aliyu, Musa Ubandawaki & Ben Ngwakwe The proposed constitutional amendment to establish State Police is facing delays in several Northern states, with many Houses of Assembly yet to receive, schedule or commence deliberations on the bill transmitted by the National Assembly. Investigations by Sunday Vanguard showed that while some assemblies have received the bill, they are yet to take a position, weeks after its transmission. Others, including Kano, Kwara, Kebbi, Taraba and Gombe, said they were yet to receive the communication from the National Assembly and therefore could not commence consideration. The bill seeks to amend the 1999 Constitution to provide for the establishment and operation of State Police Services as part of efforts to decentralise policing and strengthen security. In Taraba, the House said it was yet to receive the harmonised version of the proposed constitutional alteration. Chairman, House Committee on Information, Nelson Len, said the Assembly could not commence consideration until the National Assembly formally transmitted the document. He assured that once received, the House would subject it to legislative scrutiny and public consultation. In Kano, the Assembly also said it was yet to receive the bill. The Speaker’s spokesman, Kamaludeen Sani Shawwai, said the House could not deliberate on a document it had not officially received. Similarly, the Kwara House of Assembly said it was yet to receive the communication from the National Assembly. Chairman, House Committee on Information and Sports, Hon. Rukayat Shittu, confirmed that the draft had not been officially transmitted to the Assembly. The Kebbi Assembly also said it had not received the communication, while Gombe lawmakers are equally yet to receive the bill. In Kogi, however, the House acknowledged receipt but has yet to deliberate on it. Deputy Clerk, Bayo Aka, said the matter could come up when the Assembly resumes from its break on October 6. In Yobe, the bill was received on September 29 but has not been listed on the Order Paper for consideration. Legal Secretary to the Assembly, Ibrahim Madaki, said: “The bill has been received by the House, but it has not yet been listed in the proceedings or Order Paper for consideration.” The Borno Assembly has received and read the bill at plenary but has yet to deliberate on it or take a position. Clerk of the House, Shettima Garba, said lawmakers needed adequate time to study its possible implications for citizens. In Adamawa, the bill has been sent to the House, but is yet to be formally presented at plenary. Chairman, House Committee on Information, Mohammed Kalam Musa, said the Speaker had briefed lawmakers about it. The Benue Assembly is also yet to commence consideration. In Nasarawa, Speaker Danladi Jatau confirmed that the House received the bill from the Clerk of the National Assembly on September 18. “Yes, we are in receipt of the State Police Bill from the Clerk of the National Assembly. We received it last Friday,” Jatau said, adding that lawmakers would study the proposal before taking the necessary legislative steps. In Zamfara, the bill has been received but no action has been taken. Speaker Bulyaminu Moriki said the Assembly was yet to schedule it for deliberation. The Sokoto Assembly has also received the bill but is yet to begin debate. Deputy Speaker Kabiru Ibrahim Kware said the proposal would be carefully studied before deliberation. “We have received the bill from the National Assembly, but we have not commenced deliberation on it yet,” he said. He added that lawmakers would analyse its provisions and implications before taking a position. In Bauchi, lawmakers confirmed receipt of the bill and constituted a committee headed by Deputy Speaker Jamilu Ummaru Dahiru to examine it. The committee was given two weeks to submit its report to the House. Plateau is currently the only Northern state identified in the report where formal consideration has commenced. The House received the communication through Governor Caleb Mutfwang, after which Majority Leader Joseph Gokum moved the motion for consideration of the State Police Bill. It was seconded by Matthew Sylvanus Kwarpo. Speaker Naanlong Daniel subsequently read the communication before the House and directed the Clerk to proceed with the first reading. S-East Assemblies yet to debate State Police Bill By Vincent Ujumadu, Steve Oko, Ugochukwu Alaribe, Chinedu, Emmanuel Iheaka & Jeff Agbodo Houses of Assembly in most South-East states have yet to commence consideration of the State Police Bill recently transmitted to state legislatures by the National Assembly. Under the constitutional amendment process, at least two-thirds of the state Houses of Assembly are required to approve the proposed amendments before they can take effect. In Anambra, the House of Assembly is yet to commence debate on the bill. However, Speakers of the five South-East Houses of Assembly, at a recent meeting in Awka, agreed in principle on the need for State Police and resolved to sustain collaboration toward achieving uniform legislative practices and improved security across the zone. A committee saddled with collating and harmonising inputs from the states is already working, sources said. In Abia, the House will take a position when lawmakers resume on October 6, Acting Clerk, Pastor Promise Onwukwe, said. He told Sunday Vanguard in Umuahia that lawmakers could not vote individually, stressing that the decision must be taken collectively on the floor. “The House is currently on recess and will resume on Tuesday, October 6. Members cannot vote in isolation; it must be done in the hallowed chambers. So, when they resume, I believe they will do the needful,” he said. A lawmaker, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said the bill was before the House for consideration and that members would vote Yes or No when the Speaker calls for it. In Enugu, the House has yet to formally introduce or deliberate on the proposed State Police legislation. Similarly, the Imo State House of Assembly, which resumed from its two-month annual recess last week, did not consider the bill during plenary. The next sitting is expected on Tuesday. Meanwhile, the Ebonyi State House of Assembly has received the bill and promised an accelerated consideration. Speaker Moses Ijie Odunwa, confirmed receipt of the bill, saying the Assembly would give it the necessary accelerated hearing and deliberation. Odunwa said the legislation was aimed at strengthening the safety and security of lives and property in Ebonyi State and Nigeria at large. The post State Police Bill hits roadblock in states appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Tight monetary policy likely to continue
items.description: KARACHI: As the world continues to grapple with uncertain oil prices, the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) is unlikely to meet its FY27 mid-term inflation target of 5-7 per cent, financial experts and analysts said. Consumer Price Index-based inflation of 10.3 per cent in September clearly indicates that industry, businesses, and the general public will bear the brunt of these cost-push inflationary pressures. Experts believe the central bank will not lower interest rates to stimulate economic activity. Instead, it will maintain a tight monetary stance to support ‘sustainable’ growth. For the past four years, the government and the SBP have been satisfied with low but sustainable growth of around 3 to 3.7 per cent—a level that creates no jobs and does not address the severe problem of 44 per cent of Pakistanis living in poverty. “There is no domestic or foreign investment, and existing industries are struggling to survive. The situation would not change unless a comprehensive economic policy is introduced to support domestic investment, which is being undermined by inflated energy prices and overall double-digit inflation,” said Amir Aziz, a manufacturer and exporter of textile made-ups. “Inflation is only one factor. Bangladesh is in a much better position, as energy costs about 7 to 8 cents per unit, compared with 14 to 16 cents in Pakistan. This gives Bangladesh an advantage over Pakistani products,” said Mr Mohammad Hasham, who recently returned home after serving the Bangladesh textile industry for 25 years as the head of some of its largest textile units. He said double-digit inflation is killing both the industry and investors, and economic activity is slowing, causing pain for the general public. Tresmark Chief Executive Faisal Mamsa said that Pakistan’s authorities reportedly expect inflation to average around 7.5pc if oil returns towards $80, and around 8.2pc if it remains near $100 per barrel. “They also expect inflation to moderate after December and argue that the current 11.5pc policy rate remains appropriate,” he said. However, many experts disagree that the SBP policy rate will remain unchanged at 11.5pc despite double-digit inflation. At the same time, the government raised cut-off yields by up to 75 basis points, with the highest at 12.49pc for the one-year tenor at Wednesday’s T-bill auction. The hike in returns on risk-free government papers reflected a possible rise in the SBP policy rate at the next Monetary Policy Committee meeting on Oct 26. Mr Mamsa said the stable rupee helps contain imported inflation. Higher domestic fuel prices allow demand and imports to adjust. “The IMF, meanwhile, continues to emphasise a more market-based exchange rate. The authorities are reluctant to reopen the imported inflation Pandora’s Box,” he said, adding that a market-based exchange rate parity does not automatically mean a weaker rupee. “If remittances remain strong, reserves continue improving, the current account stays manageable, and the dollar demand remains contained, price discovery can still produce a stable currency,” he said. Published in Dawn, October 4th, 2026

items.title: Kodua dismisses rift fears, says he and John Boadu are focused on NPP victory
items.description: New Patriotic Party (NPP) General Secretary Justin Frimpong Kodua has dismissed concerns about a possible strained relationship between him and aspiring National Chairman John Boadu. According to Mr Kodua, the two are mature politicians who understand the need to work together to return the NPP to power. His comments follow concerns about how the two could work together after Mr Boadu lost the General Secretary position to Mr Kodua at the party’s 2022 national delegates conference. Provisional results from the latest conference indicate that Mr Boadu has emerged as the leading candidate in the National Chairman race. Speaking to Channel One TV, Mr Kodua said the party’s priority must be to win the 2028 general election and secure victory for its flagbearer, Dr Mahamudu Bawumia. “The positive aspect of it is that JB never stood anywhere and said that he can’t work with me. Likewise, I never stood anywhere and said I cannot work with JB,” he said. “So there shouldn’t be any problem. People are entitled to make their own assumptions and estimations. But for us, there’s no issue. We are all mature politicians. We understand that, yes, where we are now, it’s the NPP that needs to win.” Mr Kodua said he and Mr Boadu share a common objective of securing victory for Dr Bawumia in the 2028 presidential election. “We all have a common agenda, which is to make Dr Mahamudu Bawumia the president of Ghana in 2029. And we are focused,” he added. He expressed confidence that Mr Boadu and the party’s incoming leadership would work with his administration to secure victory for the NPP. “I can tell that JB and the JFK administration are going to give us victory in 2028,” he said.

items.title: Parents of abducted corps members beg Olubadan: We can’t raise N1bn ransom
items.description: By Adeola Badaru & Dickson Omobola Parents of the 20 abducted prospective National Youth Service Corps members, PCMs, were thrown into profound sadness, yesterday, leading them to appeal to the Olubadan of Ibadanland, Oba Rashidi Ladoja, to assist in rescuing their children from the kidnappers’ den. The distraught parents, who visited Ladoja at his private residence in Bodija, Ibadan, along with the Commissioner of Police in Oyo State, Olugbenga Abimbola, and the Aseyin of Iseyinland, Oba Sefiu Adeyeri, said the kidnappers threatened to kill the victims if they did not pay the N1 billion ransom within 24 hours. This came on a day when the Inspector-General of Police, IGP, Olatunji Disu, deployed the Deputy Inspector-General of Police in charge of Operations, DIG Shehu Nadada, to Imo State to coordinate the rescue of the PCMs and other abducted passengers. Last Thursday, gunmen attacked the 20 PCMs, who had travelled from Ibadan, the Oyo State capital, along the Owerri-Onitsha Road in Umunoha, Imo State, while on their way to NYSC orientation camps in different vehicles. Accusation Some of their parents accused the transport company that conveyed them from Ibadan of allegedly withholding vital passenger information when they approached its office for assistance. The parents alleged that when they visited Eduak King Transport Company in Samonda, Ibadan, in a desperate search for information that could help them contact other affected families, the company refused to provide the list of next of kin of passengers aboard the ill-fated vehicle. One of the affected mothers, Mrs Iyabo Akande, whose daughter, Kehinde Akande, was among the abducted graduates, called on the Inspector-General of Police and the government to investigate the transport operator and ensure that those found culpable were held accountable. She said: “Please, our government and the Inspector-General of Police should help us investigate the transport company, Eduak King, located at Samonda, and put fear into them. Call them to order. “Yesterday morning at their office, we were asking for the next-of-kin list so we could contact other parents, but they refused to present it or assist us. They must be held accountable.” Another parent, Olawale Olaleye, whose daughter was also among the victims, expressed concern over what he described as the company’s continued transport operations despite the abduction and the distress the incident had caused the affected families. According to him, the parents were surprised to find the company loading another vehicle when they visited its premises to seek information and assistance. He said: “We went to Samonda, to Eduak King. Surprisingly, they were already loading another vehicle. People are complaining. The company should be held liable.” Plea to Olubadan But speaking at the Olubadan’s residence, yesterday, Alhaja Akande and Oyebola Akande, who spoke on behalf of the families, said the kidnappers had been calling since Friday, demanding N50 million for each victim. “They have been calling us since yesterday (Friday) with a demand for N50 million ransom each. They are threatening that anything untoward will happen to our children if we fail to heed their request,” the parents pleaded. “There is no way we can raise such an amount at this time. Baba, kindly assist us. Don’t let them kill our children.” They appealed to the Olubadan and the police commissioner to intervene urgently, expressing fears that the lives of their children could be in danger if the abductors carried out their threats. Responding to the appeal, Oba Ladoja assured the families that concerted efforts were being made by security agencies to rescue the abducted graduates alive and unhurt. He said: “I want to assure you that your children will be rescued unharmed. We will relay whatever information we gather to you. The police are working round the clock to secure their rescue. Don’t worry yourself; the police are up to the task, and nothing will happen to your children.” Also speaking, the Oyo State Commissioner of Police, Olugbenga Abimbola, disclosed that he had been in constant communication with his counterpart in Imo State since the incident occurred, expressing confidence that the victims would be rescued safely. “I had already contacted the Imo State CP. We have been talking since the day of the incident, and he assured me that the victims would be rescued unhurt,” he said. However, the police commissioner did not disclose whether any ransom had been paid by the families or provide specific details of the ongoing rescue operations. Deployment Meanwhile, the Force Public Relations Officer, CSP Anietie Iniedu, in a statement, yesterday, said IGP Disu had deployed the Deputy Inspector-General of Police in charge of Operations, DIG Shehu Nadada, to Imo State to coordinate the rescue operation. Iniedu said the DIG arrived in Imo State with two Commissioners of Police and conducted an on-the-spot assessment of the situation and the ongoing search-and-rescue efforts. He said the DIG also reviewed the operational strategies, deployment of personnel and operational assets, and provided further directives to strengthen the coordinated response. The police spokesperson noted that the assessment was conducted alongside the Imo State Commissioner of Police, Audu Bosso; the Commissioner of Police, Federal Operations, Akpan Anifiok; the Commissioner of Police in charge of the Police Mobile Force; as well as other service commanders and members of the Management Team of the Imo State Police Command. Iniedu added: “The police are working in close coordination with sister security agencies to ensure the safe rescue of the abducted persons and the apprehension of the perpetrators. The DIG Operations, DIG Shehu Umar Nadada, assured members of the public that the Nigeria Police Force is committed to securing the safe rescue of the 20 abducted persons and will sustain the operation until the mission is successfully concluded. “He urged members of the public and the media to remain calm and vigilant and encouraged anyone with credible information that could assist the operation to promptly contact the police or the nearest security formation. All information received will be treated with strict confidentiality. Further updates will be issued as the operation progresses.” The post Parents of abducted corps members beg Olubadan: We can’t raise N1bn ransom appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Why Canada is preparing for a (long shot) US invasion
items.description: Prime Minister Mark Carney admitted last week that he has prepared for a once-unthinkable scenario – a US invasion. Noting the risk was low and the likelihood highly improbable, he told the New York Times he had a responsibility to consider all possibilities as the US-Canada relationship is redefined under the Donald Trump presidency. “That’s just risk management,” Carney said. Trump’s global tariffs and his often-repeated desire to make Canada the 51st state has led Canada to war game an attack by the Americans. In 2025, the US president said it was “highly unlikely” that the US would ever use force against Canada. Instead he said, he would continue to exert economic pressures to obtain political aims. “President Trump has done more than anyone to protect the great people of Canada,” the White House told the BBC in a statement this week. Military experts who spoke to the BBC also think an invasion is a long shot, pointing to the multiple ways the two countries work together on defence. But the issue is clearly weighing on Canadians’ minds. In January, after the US captured Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela, a Leger poll suggested that over 30% of Canadians believed that a US invasion was likely. Why it is unlikely to happen A war between Canada and the US would be complicated and almost difficult to imagine, said Lt-Gen Christopher Coates, a former military officer of 34 years with the Royal Canadian Air Force who held various senior positions. “I was involved in military operations for my whole career, and we never considered the possibility that there would be a military attack coming from US territory,” he told the BBC. Coates, who had served on Nato missions, noted that Canada and the US collaborate on many aspects of military defence. They are both members of the north Atlantic defence alliance, which mandates members to defend a fellow member-nation should they be attacked. The two countries also conduct joint Arctic defence missions under the North American Aerospace Defence Command (NORAD), and frequently share intelligence. Because of this, Coates said he believes an attack by the US on Canada would not begin with an armed assault, but rather with more discreet means like cyberwarfare. Not always the best of friends After World War II, Canada and the US became natural allies for the latter part of the 20th Century, and have become heavily integrated economically, militarily and culturally. But it wasn’t always this way. In fact, a core tenet of Canada’s identity is its resistance to US expansionism in the 18th and 19th Centuries, said Tim Foran, a researcher with the Canadian War Museum. “Fear of the United States is foundational to the political project that is Canada,” he said. Canada was formed as a collection of British North American colonies that remained loyal to the British Crown when the colonies in the modern-day US rebelled. Before the formation of Canada, the US had attempted to invade British North American colonies, taking control of Montreal in 1775 and nearly conquering Quebec City. In the war of 1812, the Americans invaded what was known then as Upper Canada, Lower Canada and the maritime colonies repeatedly, resulting in a stalemate. During that war, British troops famously burned down the White House in retaliation. Foran said that at the time, the colonies that later became Canada relied on Great Britain and its Royal Navy for its defence, as well as indigenous peoples who served as generals in major battles. Canada again contemplated war with the US after World War I in response to the US’s growing power and influence. It drafted a plan that was informed by secret trips to border cities made by Canadian army generals, who would pose as tourists and snap photos of bridges and highways for intelligence. They also spoke to local residents to better understand their enemy. A war was an unlikely scenario then, said Andrew Burtch, a researcher with the Canadian War Museum with expertise on Canada in the 20th Century, but the Canadians still wanted to be prepared. “That’s part of what militaries do,” he said. “They envisage all sorts of different scenarios.” Canada-US relations have deteriorated under the second Trump presidency. What a US invasion could look like Even if a US invasion is extremely unlikely, Matthew Schmidt, an associate professor of national security at the University of New Haven in Connecticut, said the fact that Canadians’ preparations were a sign of just how drastically the global order has shifted. He added Canadian leaders do have hard questions to ask about how closely they want to continue working with the American military – a partnership that gives them valuable information should they want to harm Canada in any way. “It’s really doing harm to relationships with the United States, and there’s a certain amount of legitimate fear,” he said. Americans might not take Trump’s comments about making Canada the 51st state seriously, he said, but Canadians clearly do – and are prepared to defend themselves if needed. So what would it be like if it happened? The first phase of a war could be quite short. According to the model used by the Canadian military, as reported on by the Globe and Mail newspaper earlier this year, a US attack would see Canada’s strategic positions overwhelmed within a week Its military would quickly be outnumbered, forcing Canadian forces to resort to guerilla-type warfare to try to suppress their enemy. Allied nations like France and Britain would be called on to provide support and defence for Canada, the newspaper reported in January, citing senior government officials. The theoretical model is believed to be the first time in a century that Canada planned for an American assault. The modelling is on the lighter end of military combat planning, Coates said. He said that Canada, unlike its Nato allies, was lagging behind when it came to having a response plan in place in the event of any ground invasion, and that it was now playing catch-up in this era of unpredictable geopolitics. Part of that, he said, was made evident by a recent call by Canada’s defence chief to drastically increase the size of its military, including the addition of as many as 300,000 lightly trained citizen soldiers. An invasion of Canada might not be straightforward from the US point of view either. Even with its outsized military, the US would have a difficult time getting buy-in for a fight with Canada, said Schmidt. “I think you would have a large number of American officers who would resign if given the order to invade Canada,” he said. “They would see it as an illegal and immoral order.” Schmidt said Canadian soldiers and American soldiers routinely train together and share a mutual respect. But in the unlikely scenario that relations would deteriorate to the point of combat, Schmidt said the US would likely focus on acquiring valuable Canadian resources like oil and minerals, and political decapitation. “You would see a kind of operation that would mirror perhaps what you saw in Venezuela,” he said, referring to US military action earlier this year to capture former Venezuelan President Maduro. Although he acknowledged the US has greater military capacity, he said that “pound for pound” Canadian soldiers would be able to put up a fight.

items.title: Cisjordanie : des soldats israéliens accusés d’avoir facilité l’accès de colons à des oliveraies palestiniennes
items.description: Des soldats israéliens ont soutenu des colons, qui se sont emparés samedi d'oliveraies palestiniennes, et plusieurs blessés ont été signalés à travers la Cisjordanie occupée, ont indiqué des témoins et des secouristes. Octobre marque le début de la récolte pour les Palestiniens, dont beaucoup considèrent les oliviers comme un symbole culturel. La saison de cette année intervient alors que la violence explose dans le territoire palestinien occupé depuis 1967, avec des attaques ou des vols quasi quotidiens perpétrés par des colons, qui bénéficient du soutien politique du gouvernement de droite de Benjamin Netanyahu, à l'approche des législatives du 27 octobre. Près du village de Beita, dans le nord de la Cisjordanie, des Palestiniens récoltant des olives dans la matinée en présence de militants solidaires, dont des Israéliens, ont fait face à des colons, qui ont brièvement reculé, ont rapporté des témoins. Des soldats sont alors intervenus, dispersant agriculteurs et militants. Ils ont arrêté plusieurs Palestiniens, dont l'un hurlait à l'intérieur d'un véhicule militaire, a constaté un journaliste de l'AFP. L'armée a aussi arrêté six journalistes, dont un de l'AFP, relâchés après vingt minutes, sans inculpation. « Comme d'habitude, nous sommes allés récolter les olives sur la terre où nous, comme nos parents et grands-parents, avons grandi et vécu », a déclaré l'un des cultivateurs, Mohammed Hamayel, à l'AFP. L'objectif de l'armée était de « dégager la zone pour que les colons puissent récolter les olives », a-t-il ajouté. Contacté par l'AFP, l'armée israélienne n'a pas commenté. Ailleurs dans le nord de la Cisjordanie, des soldats israéliens ont tiré des gaz lacrymogènes sur des cultivateurs dans des oliveraies, déclenchant des incendies sur les terres desséchées, a constaté un journaliste de l'AFP. Selon le Croissant-Rouge palestinien, 12 Palestiniens ont été hospitalisés après avoir été battus par des colons lors de cinq incidents distincts dans la journée. Jeudi et vendredi, deux Palestiniens ont été tués par des colons, selon des responsables palestiniens. Ces violences suscitent une réprobation internationale croissante. Londres a notamment imposé des sanctions visant les produits issus des colonies en Cisjordanie, illégales au regard du droit international. Benjamin Netanyahu a attribué ces attaques à « une poignée de jeunes délinquants, environ 150 ». Selon un décompte de l'AFP fondé sur les données du ministère palestinien de la Santé, l'armée et des colons ont tué en Cisjordanie plus de 1.100 Palestiniens, combattants ou civils depuis le début de la guerre à Gaza, en octobre 2023. D'après les chiffres israéliens, sur la même période, près de 50 Israéliens – civils et membres des forces de sécurité – ont été tués dans des attaques palestiniennes ou lors d'opérations militaires israéliennes. The post Cisjordanie : des soldats israéliens accusés d’avoir facilité l’accès de colons à des oliveraies palestiniennes appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: FAO flags gaps in Pakistan’s nutritious food supply
items.description: • UN agency says over 60pc of citizens unable to afford healthy diet • Calls for overhaul of agrifood system ISLAMABAD: The Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) of the United Nations has emphasised the urgent need to transform Pakistan’s agrifood system to improve access to healthy diets, a critical step towards addressing all forms of malnutrition and their related costs to society. The UN agency, in its latest assessment on “Food Supply for Healthy Diets in Pakistan”, observed that a major challenge in the country’s current food supply is the persistent mismatch between the quantities of food available and those required for the population to consume a healthy diet aligned with the national food-based dietary guidelines (FBDGs). “Enabling access to healthy diets for all is essential to achieving Pakistan’s national development priorities. Yet over 60 per cent of Pakistanis cannot afford a healthy diet, contributing to the high rates of malnutrition across the country. At the same time, diet-related non-communicable diseases (NCD) are rising, while various forms of undernutrition persist. Unhealthy diets are a common cause of all forms of malnutrition and contribute directly to morbidity and mortality from NCD,” the assessment shows. The FAO listed priority policy actions to strengthen demand for healthy diets through consumer-focused policies; updating Pakistan’s FBDGs to reflect nutrition, health, and environmental priorities and use it for nutrition education and behavior change; introducing evidence-based fiscal measures, including taxes on sugar-sweetened beverages and other foods high in sugar, salt, and unhealthy fats; introducing front-of-pack nutrition labelling to help consumers make informed food choices; protecting vulnerable populations; restricting the marketing of unhealthy foods, particularly those targeting children, expanding nutritious school meal programmes; and strengthening social protection programmes to improve access to nutritious foods. The assessment recommended reorienting the agrifood system to deliver healthy diets, aligning agricultural policies and investment priorities to increase support for the production of vegetables, fruits, pulses, roots and tubers across the country, while supporting milk production in some regions; and providing greater incentives for food processors to meet food safety and quality standards and reformulate foods to reduce salt, sugar and unhealthy fats. It called for promoting healthier retail food environments, through investments in storage, cold chains, and market infrastructure to reduce losses. These actions, combined with regular monitoring, can contri­bute to increasing access to and consumption of healthy diets in Paki­stan, both today and in the future. The FAO assessment says large gaps were observed for several nutritious food groups, particularly vegetables, roots and tubers, fruits, and legumes and pulses. However, important misalignment exists between Pakistan’s dietary guidelines and food supply, with supply gaps for several nutritious food groups, particularly vegetables, roots and tubers, fruits, legumes and pulses, while the supply for staples and sugar exceeds what is needed for healthy diets. “Enabling equitable access to diverse, nutritious, safe, and affordable foods that support healthy diets is a policy imperative for Pakistan,” the assessment said. Published in Dawn, October 4th, 2026

items.title: Fear of electoral violence in 2027, by Tonnie Iredia
items.description: Since December 12, 1959 when the first national pre-independence elections were held in Nigeria till today, we have had no election without citizens losing sleep and remaining exceedingly anxious over electoral violence. Even the June 12, 1993 Presidential election internationally recognised as the nation’s best had its own tension. Indeed, the 1993 election was the first to be annulled in the nation’s history. Nigerian elections have always been subjected to a plethora of electoral malpractices featuring political intimidation, vote buying and collusion of the electoral body with interest groups to rig our polls. These anomalies have greatly discouraged citizen participation in elections leading to sequential decline in voter turn-out. With the introduction of technology and flashes of occasional above average performance of the Independent National Electoral Commission INEC voters started nursing the hope that perhaps failed elections were soon to end – an enthusiastic feeling that was dashed by the inexplicable technical glitch that marred the 2023 Presidential contest. Painfully, the National Assembly that should have rekindled the hope of citizens by redressing the loopholes in the Electoral Act lost the golden opportunity of making history. Its members rather than holding the bull by its horn through a seamless reform of enthroning real time electronic transmission of results decided to play politics. They used a tiny thread to tie the bull’s horn allowing the people to believe that their votes may not count in 2027. Since then, everyone has chosen to embrace self-help. While those in the ruling party are busy intimidating others because they happen to be in control of the instruments of coercion, the opposition parties are tidying up arrangements to muster enough courage to meet force with force. Already, the vow of the opposition parties that the 2027 elections will be won and lost at the polling centres gravely throws a spanner into our democracy with the suggestion that there is nothing just about the official framework for justice delivery. The summary of what we have said so far is that in 2027, there will be fierce fighting between two elephants which will result in the deaths of not the combatants and their families but the poor and ordinary masses of society. In which case, there is already fear and anxiety among our people over heavy political violence in 2027. Anyone who is in doubt should go back to our media records that are replete with reports of preparations for violence by our political class. One report for example, will show that Nigeria has become the first and most likely the only country where massively voting can kill some contestants. A senator of the federal republic Francis Fadahunsi (Osun East) who said it insisted that he didn’t say anyone should be killed through inflicting bodily harm or physical attack but through massive voting that can easily send Osun politicians into untimely death. Nothing was done to the senator to whom such an unacceptable rhetoric was credited. In Kuje, an area council of the federal capital territory, the people were lucky that they got an early signal that anyone unwilling to support the APC should just quit the council area. If a leader like Samuel Shekwolo or his type assumes the chairmanship of Kuje Area Council or indeed any of the FCT council areas, then elections in such location would be based on the import of the directive of Shekwolo to citizens that “It’s either you are doing APC or leave the area council.” What would happen to those not supporting the ruling party is more specific in Borno state where the Commissioner for Youth and Sports Development Sainna Buba reportedly used threatening language while addressing an APC-linked political gathering. On the occasion, Buba was quoted to have said that those who “show us a finger” would have their fingers broken and those who refused to follow the government would be “flogged.” Whether in Kuje or Borno, nothing was done to those who have used their might to breach the Nigerian constitution which guarantees to every citizen, freedom of association as well as freedom of expression. The several pleas by political analysts to higher authorities to call their supporters and officials to order are simplistic because in many cases the same higher authorities are behind the threats. In Kebbi State, the chairman of Gwandu Local Government Area, Alhaji Atiku Ahmad Mandiya, was captured in a video telling supporters that anyone who spoke against Governor Nasir Idris “should be dealt with.” As if to confirm that the message came directly from above, Mandiya also specifically promised to secure the release of any supporter arrested for confronting the governor’s opponents. In Ebonyi State, it was the governor himself, Francis Nwifuru who warned newly inaugurated local government chairmen that they could be removed if they failed to deliver their councils to the APC in 2027. In a swift response to allegations that APC members were harassing and intimidating political critics, Nwifuru said “any chairman who fails to win his council will be removed from office and replaced with a councillor. I want this information to be on the headlines of newspapers because, as politicians, we will not speak in secret.” The above explains why the newly sworn-in Chairman of Ohaukwu Local Government Area, Eze Paul Ituma, warned residents in his area who were unwilling to align with the APC to stay away from the area. The media had indeed reported Ituma’s pledge to implement governor Nwifuru’s directive after his warning that opposition elements who wanted to challenge Nwifuru or reject the ruling APC should stay away from the council area. Ohaukwu according to the LGA chair has no room for individuals opposed to the governor or the APC, stressing that such persons would be treated as “enemies” and declared “persona non grata” in the council area. In nearby Enugu state, the situation was not different. Gunmen allegedly associated with the ruling party had disrupted a meeting of the People’s Democratic Party (PDP) in Akpugo Ward 3, Nkanu West Local Government Area. According to media reports, ‘canopies, chairs and several other items brought for the meeting were shattered or destroyed by the attackers, while those attending the meeting were said to have fled to safety.’ What other type of evidence do we need to appreciate the fragility of our nation where a set of contestants can determine what their opponents are allowed to do in a supposed democracy where everyone is equal before the law and where there is a level-playing field for all the recognized teams. To make matters worse, none of those intimidating others has been sanctioned for refusing to play the game by the rules. The only person who is on record to have apologised for his act was the Yobe state chairman of the APC Alhaji Mohammed Gadaka, who had told women at a rally to divorce their anti-APC husbands if they prevented them from voting for the APC. Gadaka made the statement while addressing hundreds of new defectors to the APC in Nangere town. He reportedly promised to personally pay the “new bride price” for any woman who ended her marriage because of her loyalty to the party. The remark as usual attracted widespread condemnation from residents, including Islamic scholars, who described it as provocative and capable of undermining family values. Following the backlash, Gadaka released a 42-second video on the Facebook page of Mamman Mohammed the Director General, Press and Media Affairs to Governor Mai Mala Buni, in which he withdrew the statement. He said his comment had been misunderstood and was merely a “joking banter” based on a long-standing tradition of playful exchanges between his Ngamo people and their Kare-Kare-speaking neighbours. In Gadaka’s words, “my statement was just a usual joking banter and does not in any way represent the ideals I stand for or intended to encourage divorce among married people.” How come all others who threatened opponents or members of the public had never been questioned? With the atmosphere that has been painted above, many leaders and relevant institutions deserve blame. The Police for instance are yet to make public statements concerning those who intercepted Peter Obi in Makurdi. They have also been silent over cases where one group disrupted the rallies of another thereby pushing those offended into looking out for revenge. The Abdulsami Peace Committee may not have had a force of law behind it to sanction breaches but having held meetings with political party leaders, it is not too much if it writes letters to offending parties to remind them of the tacit agreements reached. Where such counselling is done the media should be briefed. In all, Nigeria needs to avoid elections where some citizens have to die so that others can be elected. The post Fear of electoral violence in 2027, by Tonnie Iredia appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Dangote’s planned Kenya refinery faces legal challenge by consumer-rights group
items.description: Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote’s $16 billion oil refinery in Kenya faces another legal challenge, this time from a ​consumer-rights group alleging that key details about the project ‌have not been made public. The Consumers Federation of Kenya (COFEK) filed a petition with the Public Private Partnerships Petition Committee, COFEK Secretary General Stephen ​Mutoro said in a post on X. It is the ​second legal hurdle for the 700,000-barrel-per-day (bpd) refinery, after more ⁠than 130 residents filed a lawsuit , saying the land in ​Lamu — where the plant is being built — is their ancestral heritage. ​A hearing on the case is due on October 14. COFEK wants any non-compliant approvals set aside for the refinery and reconsidered. It wants details about ​the government’s plan to take a stake in the ​refinery to be disclosed, such as the acquisition vehicle, share class and payment ‌terms ⁠and evidence that there was public participation, among other things. A Dangote Group spokesperson declined to comment. A Kenyan government spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment. When he broke ​ground to start ​construction on ⁠Wednesday, Dangote shrugged off the land rights claim and expressed confidence the refinery would go ahead, ​saying: “Anybody who wants to cause trouble, we ​are ready.” Dangote ⁠is looking to replicate his group’s 700,000 bpd refinery in Nigeria. He has offered regional governments a combined 30% stake in ⁠the ​Lamu refinery, which is scheduled to ​be completed in 2030.

items.title: Sanaa, Riyadh rattled by strikes as war widens
items.description: • Houthis say Saudi aircraft carried out 26 strikes on Yemen capital, claim attack on Aramco facility in south of Riyadh • Trump’s top national security aides meet secretly on Yemen, Iran SANAA: Fighting between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis showed no signs of abating on Saturday, with the Houthis saying the kingdom had launched dozens of strikes on capital Sanaa, while flames and smoke were seen rising from a facility belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco, south of Riyadh. While Houthis later said they attacked an Aramco facility with ballistic missiles and drones, there was no immediate confirmation from Saudi Arabia. The foes have traded strikes since the Houthis seized all of Yemen’s Red Sea coast and took control of the Bab al-Mandab strait in a lightning offensive. US media outlet Axios reported earlier on Friday that US President Donald Trump’s top cabinet members “met secretly at the presidential retreat at Camp David to discuss the Saudi-Houthi conflict in Yemen and next steps in the Iran war ”. Vice President Vance chaired the meeting, the news outlet reported, citing people familiar with the matter. Houthi-affiliated Al-Masirah TV reported that Saudi aircraft hit Sanaa with 26 strikes, after earlier reporting “Saudi aggression” against the Yemeni capital, without providing details on the targets or casualties. Two AFP correspondents in Sanaa reported hearing loud explosions and seeing warplanes firing missiles on the city. In neighbouring Saudi Arabia, flames and smoke were seen rising on Saturday afternoon from a facility belonging to state-owned oil giant Aramco south of Riyadh, an AFP journalist said, although both the Houthis and Saudi authorities had yet to comment. The circumstances remained unclear, though the Houthis have claimed several attacks on facilities belonging to Aramco, majority-owned by the Saudi state, in recent months. The journalist reported seeing firefighters attempting to extinguish a blaze at the energy giant’s Riyadh refinery, located south of the capital, while ambulances and police vehicles were stationed near the facility. Al-Masirah TV earlier on Saturday also reported missile strikes on the telecommunications network in Yemen’s northwestern governorate of Saada, one of the group’s strongholds. It comes after the Houthis said that Saudi Arabia bombed the Yemeni capital itself on Thursday night for the first time since renewed fighting broke out between the two sides in July. The health ministry in Sanaa claims 72 people have been killed and 125 wounded in Saudi attacks on Yemen since the escalation began, Al Jazeera reports citing the Al Masirah news outlet. Hunger warning After several years of calm, Yemen was plunged back into civil war that month, pitting the Houthis, who control most of northwest Yemen including Sanaa, against Yemen’s internationally recognised government. The government, based in the city of Aden, controls much of the country’s south and east — a region that is larger but much less populated. Hostilities were reignited after four years of a fragile truce when Iran sent a plane to Sanaa carrying a Houthi delegation. The flight did not seek authorisation from Saudi Arabia, contravening a practice in place for a decade. Riyadh retaliated with strikes on Sanaa airport, and in response the Houthis attacked Saudi territory for the first time since 2022. Since then, fighting has intensified with the Houthis launching a lightning offensive in which they seized control of coastal regions along the Bab al-Mandab strait. They have also struck multiple Saudi targets including oil infrastructure and the capital Riyadh while also announcing a naval blockade on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea. Appalling conditions The renewed fighting has worsened the already appalling humanitarian conditions in Yemen, one of the world’s poorest countries, with the World Food Programme warning on Friday that three-quarters of the population was unable to meet its basic food needs. Fighting in recent days has centred on Taiz, where dozens of combatants were reported killed on Friday by sources on both sides. The Houthis reported 55 of their fighters had been killed while government sources told AFP that 26 troops had died. The battle for Taiz is taking place on several fronts, including highlands overlooking coastal areas recently seized by the Houthis. While the Houthis have conquered swathes of territory, they have yet to wrest control of Taiz city, which is Yemen’s third-largest after Sanaa and Aden. The Houthis also on Friday said Saudi Arabia had launched 94 strikes against areas under their control in the past 24 hours. Saudi authorities meanwhile reported a Houthi projectile had damaged a school in the city of Najran near the Yemen border. Published in Dawn, October 4th, 2026

items.title: Hawa Koomson stands by pepper spray plan, vows to bring rival on board
items.description: Former Awutu Senya East MP, Mavis Hawa Koomson, has defended her proposal to provide pepper spray to women of the New Patriotic Party (NPP), insisting she has no regrets about the pledge. Speaking after she was said to have won her election as the party’s National Women’s Organiser at the NPP National Delegates Conference in Kumasi on Saturday, October 3, she said the proposal was intended to help women protect themselves rather than encourage confrontation. Hawa Koomson said her personal experience during the violence at the Ablekuma North parliamentary rerun had reinforced her belief that women should have access to tools for self-defence. “I’m not retracting it. I’m not sure it’s a crime to give someone a pepper spray to defend himself. I’m a living testimony. When I was beaten at Ablekuma North, it was the pepper spray that saved my life.” She maintained that her position had not changed despite criticism of the proposal. “I have no regret, and I’m not retracting it. They can talk otherwise. That’s my thinking,” she said. Koomson also pledged to work to advance the interests of women in the NPP following her election. Asked what she intended to do for the party’s women, she attributed her victory and future plans to her faith. “The Lord is my strength. He who has given me the victory will guide me. He will lead me and provide for me.” Her election followed a contest for the National Women’s Organiser position at the party’s National Delegates Conference in Kumasi. The final ballot featured Koomson and Hajia Safia Mohammed. Despite the contest, Koomson said she would work with her opponent and involve her in the affairs of the women’s wing. She rejected the suggestion that the election had been particularly difficult, saying she did not consider it a tough contest. However, she said the outcome would not prevent her from reaching out to her opponent. “It was never a tough contest. No, I didn’t see it as a tough contest. But what I’m saying is that I’ll bring her on board since we are all MPP members. We are all going to work for the party. Party and nothing else.” Describing her opponent as her “daughter”, Koomson said she intended to involve her in the work ahead. “She’s my daughter. Ah, she can’t say that I’m her mother. So she’s my daughter. I’ll bring her on board and be sending her. I will send her on errands. That’s what I’m going to do.” Koomson’s comments come as the NPP begins a new phase following its national officers’ elections, with the newly elected executives expected to take charge of the party’s organisational affairs.

items.title: ‘There is no competition’ – Justin Kodua confident of NPP General Secretary re-election
items.description: Incumbent General Secretary of the New Patriotic Party (NPP), Justin Frimpong Kodua, has expressed confidence in retaining his position, saying feedback from delegates across the country suggests he faces little competition. Speaking on the sidelines of the NPP National Delegates Conference in Kumasi on Sunday, October 4, Mr Kodua said his assessment was based on engagements with party delegates during his campaign across the 16 regions. “There is no competition. There’s no competition because, as I went around the 16 regions, that was the feedback from the party delegates, and they spoke with emotion. They spoke their mind that they know the work I’ve done for the party, and certainly didn’t see this as a contest,” he said. According to Mr Kodua, reports from his agents at the conference suggested that his re-election could effectively amount to an acclamation. He expressed gratitude to party members for the confidence they had shown in his leadership. The General Secretary contest was among the national executive positions being decided by NPP delegates at the Baba Yara Sports Stadium in Kumasi. Four candidates were listed for the position, including Mr Kodua, Eugene Boakye Antwi, Sylvester Tetteh and Dr Charles Dwamena. Mr Kodua also linked his campaign to the NPP’s broader political objective, expressing his expectation that Dr Mahamudu Bawumia would lead the party into the 2028 general election. “…inshallah, by the time we get to 2029, Dr Mohammad Bawumia will become the president of this country,” he said. Asked what party members should expect from him if retained as General Secretary, Mr Kodua pledged to work with the other national executives on the basis of teamwork and discipline. “Well, they should expect teamwork based on discipline, and I’m looking forward to the other executive that they are going to elect. So that we all sit down and work hard.” He said the priority for the incoming national executives would be to prepare the party for the next general election. “The only thing the party expects from us is to win the elections in 2028. That I can assure you, we work towards it,” he said. The NPP’s national officers’ elections form the final stage of the party’s nationwide reorganisation ahead of the 2028 general election. More than 7,000 delegates were expected to participate in the exercise.

In a fiercely contested fought title match, Kolesova and Ndukwu played best when it mattered most to seal the title defeating the Chapepa sisters 7-6(4), 6-3. Milan Kolesolva and Alisha Ndukwa [1] are the Girls’ Doubles champions. In the boys’ doubles match, Mannan Ashok Agarwal and Dev Vipul Patel [1] sealed a memorable week by taking home the championship. The Indian duo booked their place in the final with a commanding 6-3, 6-2 performance against David Beckles and Ziao Qian. Facing Om Verma [2] and Zayyan Virani in the final, Agarwal and Patel showed strength in the deciding match tiebreak to close out a 6-1, 3-6, 10-4 victory to claim the J100 Accra title. items.title: Chinese envoy: China urges improved global human rights governance
items.description: China has called on the international community to establish a just, equitable and inclusive global human rights governance system guided by the Global Governance Initiative. Jia Guide, China's permanent representative to the UN Office at Geneva and other international organizations in Switzerland, made the remarks on Wednesday while delivering a joint statement entitled "Improving International Human Rights Governance," on behalf of 71 countries at the 63rd session of the Human Rights Council at the Palais des Nations. The Global Governance Initiative, proposed by Chinese President Xi Jinping on September 1, 2025, has received support and positive responses from numerous countries and international organizations. Jia noted in the joint statement that the international landscape is undergoing profound changes amid a complex and turbulent environment, while global human rights governance is facing profound adjustments. He said that China puts forward four proposals: First, adopt a people-centered approach. It is up to the people of each country to assess and improve their own human rights situation, so as to stay true to the original aspiration of human rights governance and meet people's needs. Second, uphold sovereign equality. All countries should participate, make decisions and benefit on an equal footing. Greater attention should be paid to the voices of the Global South. China advocates fairness, objectivity and non-selectivity, and calls for dialogue and cooperation based on mutual respect. Third, uphold fairness and justice. China opposes the politicization and instrumentalization of human rights, takes a holistic approach to all categories of human rights, advances human rights reform in a prudent manner, and supports multilateral human rights institutions and experts in discharging their mandates objectively and impartially. Fourth, uphold the international rule of law. China champions the purposes and principles of the UN Charter, ensures the equal and consistent application of international law and international rules, and opposes double standards, interference in the internal affairs of other countries under the pretext of human rights, and imposition of one's own standards on others. The joint statement is based on the platform of The Group of Friends of Global Governance in Geneva, officially launched on February 27, 2026, at the Palais des Nations.
